sharpe.label: Sharpe ratio
sharpe.short: Return earned for each unit of risk taken.
sharpe.body: For every unit of price swing this investment put you through, it returned this many units of return above cash. It treats upside and downside swings as equally bad, which is why we show Sortino next to it.
sharpe.scale: Above 1.0 is generally considered good, above 2.0 excellent.
sharpe.caveat: Sharpe ratios estimated over a few years carry a lot of uncertainty — the range shown after the ± is the 95% confidence interval. If two investments' ranges overlap heavily, the difference between them is probably noise.

sortino.label: Sortino ratio
sortino.short: Return earned for each unit of downside risk taken.
sortino.body: Like Sharpe, but only counts downward swings as risk. Upside surprises don't count against it. Usually higher than Sharpe; a Sortino much higher than the Sharpe means most of this investment's volatility was to the upside.
sortino.scale: Above 1.0 is generally considered good, above 2.0 excellent.

calmar.label: Calmar ratio
calmar.short: Annual return per unit of worst drawdown.
calmar.body: How much annual return you got for the worst peak-to-trough fall you would have lived through. The most intuitive risk-adjusted ratio: return per unit of worst pain.
calmar.scale: Above 0.5 is decent, above 1.0 is strong.

martin.label: Martin ratio (UPI)
martin.short: Annual return per unit of the Ulcer Index.
martin.body: Like Calmar, but uses the whole drawdown path — how deep and how long — rather than just the single worst point. A more complete picture of how uncomfortable the ride was.
martin.scale: Higher is better; compare it only against other instruments over the same period.

volatility.label: Volatility
volatility.short: How much the price swings, annualised.
volatility.body: The annualised standard deviation of daily returns. Shown for reference, but deliberately not the headline risk figure here — research shows investors feel drawdowns, not day-to-day wiggle, so we lead with max drawdown instead.

maxDrawdown.label: Max drawdown
maxDrawdown.short: The worst peak-to-trough fall over this period.
maxDrawdown.body: If you had bought at the worst possible moment, this is how far down you would have been before it recovered — the single number that best predicts whether a real investor would have panic-sold.

timeUnderWater.label: Time under water
timeUnderWater.short: How long it took to get back to even.
timeUnderWater.body: The span from the prior peak to full recovery. This is the number that actually determines whether a retail investor capitulates — not the depth of the fall, but how long they'd have had to wait it out.

ulcerIndex.label: Ulcer Index
ulcerIndex.short: A single number for how deep and how long the drawdowns were.
ulcerIndex.body: Squares each day's drawdown depth before averaging, so it penalises deep, prolonged declines far more than brief dips — closer to how a loss actually feels than plain volatility.

var95.label: Value at Risk (95%)
var95.short: The threshold for a bad-but-not-worst day.
var95.body: On the worst 1 day in 20 over this period, the loss was at least this large. It says nothing about how much worse the remaining 5% of days could get — see CVaR for that.

cvar95.label: Expected shortfall (95%)
cvar95.short: The average loss on the worst days.
cvar95.body: The average loss across only the worst 5% of days — answers "and when it is that bad, how bad on average?". Strictly more informative than VaR alone.

beta.label: Beta
beta.short: How much this moves for each 1% move in the benchmark.
beta.body: A beta of 1.2 means it typically moved 1.2% when the benchmark moved 1%.
beta.caveat: Always check the R² next to it: if R² is low, the benchmark explains very little of this instrument's movement and the beta isn't telling you much.

alpha.label: Alpha (annualised)
alpha.short: Return left over after accounting for market exposure.
alpha.body: The annualised return this instrument produced beyond what its beta to the benchmark would predict.
alpha.caveat: A single-factor alpha against one benchmark is not strong evidence of skill — check its own confidence interval and R² before reading much into it.

rSquared.label: R²
rSquared.short: How much of the movement the benchmark actually explains.
rSquared.body: The share of this instrument's variance explained by the benchmark in the beta/alpha regression. Professionals always check this next to beta — a beta from a regression with low R² is mostly noise.

upCapture.label: Up capture
upCapture.short: How much of the benchmark's up days this captured.
upCapture.body: On days the benchmark rose, this instrument captured this percentage of that move on average.

downCapture.label: Down capture
downCapture.short: How much of the benchmark's down days this captured.
downCapture.body: On days the benchmark fell, this instrument captured this percentage of that fall on average. Lower is better here — it means smaller losses on the benchmark's bad days.

informationRatio.label: Information ratio
informationRatio.short: Active return per unit of tracking error versus the benchmark.
informationRatio.body: The right way to answer "was this better than the index, and how consistently?" — active return divided by how much that return varied.

trackingError.label: Tracking error
trackingError.short: How much this instrument's return diverges from the benchmark's.
trackingError.body: The annualised volatility of the return difference between this instrument and the benchmark. A near-index fund has a tracking error close to zero.

correlation.label: Correlation
correlation.short: How closely two instruments move together.
correlation.body: From −1 to +1. Above about 0.8 means holding both gives you much less diversification than it looks like — they will usually move together.
correlation.scale: Below 0.3 is meaningfully diversifying; above 0.8 is close to redundant.

downsideCorrelation.label: Downside correlation
downsideCorrelation.short: Correlation measured only on the benchmark's worst days.
downsideCorrelation.body: Diversification matters most exactly when things go wrong, and correlations usually rise in a crash.
downsideCorrelation.caveat: If this number is much higher than the headline correlation, these two won't protect you when it counts.

diversificationRatio.label: Diversification ratio
diversificationRatio.short: How much combining these actually reduced risk.
diversificationRatio.body: The weighted average of each instrument's own volatility, divided by the volatility of holding them together in equal weight. A ratio well above 1.0 means real diversification benefit; near 1.0 means holding them together barely helped.

cagr.label: CAGR
cagr.short: Compound annual growth rate over this period.
cagr.body: The constant annual growth rate that would take the starting price to the ending price over this exact span, on a calendar-day basis so periods of different lengths are comparable.

cumulativeReturn.label: Cumulative return
cumulativeReturn.short: Total return over the whole period, uncompounded to a yearly rate.
cumulativeReturn.body: How much a single investment made or lost from the start of the period to the end, including dividends.

trailingPe.label: Trailing P/E
trailingPe.short: Price divided by the last 12 months of earnings.
trailingPe.body: How many years of current earnings you're paying for at today's price. Always read against a peer or sector reference — a P/E of 28 means nothing on its own.
trailingPe.caveat: Undefined or misleading when earnings are negative or unusually depressed/inflated.

forwardPe.label: Forward P/E
forwardPe.short: Price divided by next year's expected earnings.
forwardPe.body: Like trailing P/E, but based on analyst estimates rather than reported results — more forward-looking, but only as reliable as the estimates behind it.
forwardPe.caveat: Depends on analyst consensus estimates, which can be wrong or sparse for smaller names.

priceToBook.label: Price to book
priceToBook.short: Price relative to accounting net asset value.
priceToBook.body: How the market values the company relative to what its balance sheet says it's worth.
priceToBook.caveat: Close to meaningless for asset-light software businesses; for financials it is often the primary valuation metric.

evToEbitda.label: EV / EBITDA
evToEbitda.short: Enterprise value relative to operating earnings.
evToEbitda.body: Capital-structure-neutral, so it compares companies fairly regardless of how much debt they carry — the multiple professionals actually use for cross-company comparison.

evToSales.label: EV / Sales
evToSales.body: The fallback valuation multiple when earnings are negative — which is exactly when P/E goes blank.

dividendYield.label: Dividend yield
dividendYield.short: Annual dividends as a percentage of price.
dividendYield.body: How much cash income the current price buys you per year, before any price change.
dividendYield.caveat: A high yield alone can be a warning sign (a "yield trap") — always check the payout ratio next to it to see whether the dividend is sustainable.

payoutRatio.label: Payout ratio
payoutRatio.short: The share of earnings paid out as dividends.
payoutRatio.body: What fraction of profit goes to dividends rather than being reinvested or retained. A ratio near or above 100% leaves little cushion if earnings dip.

fcfYield.label: Free cash flow yield
fcfYield.short: Free cash flow as a percentage of market value.
fcfYield.body: Free cash flow is harder to manipulate with accounting choices than reported earnings, and it's defined even when P/E is not (negative earnings).

roe.label: Return on equity
roe.short: Profit generated per unit of shareholder equity.
roe.body: A quality measure: how efficiently the company turns shareholders' capital into profit.
roe.caveat: Leverage inflates ROE mechanically — always check debt/equity alongside it.

debtToEquity.label: Debt / equity
debtToEquity.short: Total debt relative to shareholder equity.
debtToEquity.body: A core solvency measure — high leverage is the single best predictor of permanent capital loss in a downturn.

expenseRatio.label: Expense ratio
expenseRatio.short: The fund's annual fee, taken automatically from its value.
expenseRatio.body: The most reliable predictor of how a fund performs against its peers — in any market, net returns equal gross returns minus costs, so the low-cost fund tends to win by arithmetic.
expenseRatio.caveat: A 1%/year difference compounds to roughly a quarter of terminal wealth over 30 years.

psr.label: Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio
psr.short: The probability the true Sharpe ratio is genuinely above zero.
psr.body: Converts a point estimate into a confidence statement, accounting for sample size, skew and fat tails — the honest version of "is this actually good, or did it just get lucky?"
psr.caveat: A statement about the past, calculated from the sample shown — not a forecast.
